title: Who ran it
lede: Roles and dates come from the filings and the Richmond Fed’s history. Where a date is missing, we found no source for it.

people.name: Samuel S. Wurtzel
people.text: Opened Wards in Richmond after hearing in a barbershop that the South’s first television station had just started there. Took the company public in 1961.[^29]

people.name: Alan L. Wurtzel
people.text: Rescued the company from near-bankruptcy in 1975 and built the superstore format.[^29]
people.later: Published “Good to Great to Gone: The 60 Year Rise and Fall of Circuit City” in 2012.[^31]

people.name: Richard L. Sharp
people.text: Took the chain from 69 stores to 616 and backed both CarMax and Divx. He was chief executive of both Circuit City and Divx when the venture closed.[^29][^33]

people.name: W. Alan McCollough
people.text: Left appliances, ended commissions and completed the CarMax separation as chairman, president and chief executive.[^29][^12]

people.name: Philip J. Schoonover
people.role: Chairman, president and CEO until Sep 22, 2008
people.text: Announced the wage management initiative in 2007. Press reports put his fiscal 2006 pay at $8.52 million.[^10][^30][^16]

people.name: James A. Marcum
people.text: Joined the board in the settlement with Wattles Capital Management and signed the liquidation announcement.[^19][^15]

people.name: Mark J. Wattles
people.text: The [Hollywood Video](/hollywood-video/) founder ran a proxy contest in 2008 and settled for three board seats.[^19]

people.name: Ronny Shmoel
people.text: Announced the 2018 return of circuitcity.com at the Consumer Electronics Show.[^36]
